summary: This Standards Track document defines the base syntax of Certificate Management over CMS, a certificate management protocol using the Cryptographic Message Syntax. It is used together with the transport document (RFC 10003) and the compliance requirements (RFC 10004). It obsoletes RFC 5272 and RFC 6402.

plainLanguage.summary:
CMC is the message format a program uses to ask a certificate authority for a certificate. It builds on the same container that signed email uses, so signing, encrypting and time stamping all come for free.

The simple form is the request anyone who has used the old PKCS #10 format already knows. The full form wraps requests in that container and attaches extra pieces, called controls, for identity checks, revocation, batch requests and the rest. Both forms are answered by a reply that says whether the request succeeded, failed, or is waiting on something.

subtitle: A message format for asking a certificate authority to issue a certificate.

tldr.problem: Certification authorities needed a way to accept key certification requests that could also carry identity checks, revocation requests and other extra services, without inventing a new message format for each.
tldr.mechanism: CMC wraps certification requests in the Cryptographic Message Syntax, which is the container used for signed email, and attaches optional pieces called controls to carry the extra services. A simple form that is just a bare certification request is kept for existing practice.
tldr.outcome: A client can ask for a certificate, prove it holds the private key, be told to wait while a human check happens, and ask for other services in the same exchange. The RFC obsoletes RFC 5272 and RFC 6402, and needs the transport and compliance documents to be complete.

sections.title: What CMC Is For
sections.content:
The document defines the base syntax for CMC, a certificate management protocol using the Cryptographic Message Syntax. The protocol addresses two immediate needs within the Internet public key infrastructure community: the need for an interface to public key certification products and services based on CMS and PKCS #10, and the need for a PKI enrollment protocol for encryption-only keys due to algorithm or hardware design.

A small number of additional services are defined to supplement the core certification request service. The document is one of three: it requires the transport document and the requirements usage document along with itself for a full definition.

The protocol must be based as much as possible on the existing CMS, PKCS #10 and Certificate Request Message Format specifications. It must support the current industry practice of a PKCS #10 certification request followed by a PKCS #7 certs-only response as a subset of the protocol. It must easily support the multi-key enrollment protocols required by S/MIME and other groups. It must supply a way of doing all enrollment operations in a single round trip, and where that is not possible the number of round trips is to be minimised. It must be designed so that all key generation can occur on the client.

Support must exist for the mandatory algorithms used by S/MIME, and should exist for all other algorithms cited by the S/MIME core documents. The protocol must contain proof-of-possession methods, with optional provisions for multiple-round-trip proof of possession if necessary. And it must support deferred and pending responses to enrollment requests, for cases where external procedures are required to issue a certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: The design rule was to reuse what already exists. If a product already speaks the signed-message format and the old request format, a certificate authority can add richer requests without a new protocol from scratch.

sections.title: The Two Kinds of Request and Response
sections.content:
A PKI enrollment transaction in this specification is generally composed of a single round trip of messages. In the simplest case a request is sent from the client to the server and a response is returned. In more complicated cases, such as delayed certificate issuance, more than one round trip is required.

There are two request types. A Simple PKI Request is the bare PKCS #10, used in the event that no other services are needed. A Full PKI Request is one or more PKCS #10, Certificate Request Message Format or other request structures wrapped in a CMS encapsulation as part of a PKIData.

There are two response types as well, both based on signed data or authenticated data. A Simple PKI Response is a certs-only signed data, used when no other services are needed. A Full PKI Response is a PKIResponse content type wrapped in signed data.

No special services are provided for renewal, meaning a new certificate with the same key, or for rekey, meaning a new certificate with a new key. Instead those requests look the same as any certification request, except that the identity and identity proof controls are absent, because the same information comes from the use of an existing certificate from a certificate authority when signing the request. The authority that issued the original certificate and the authority the request is made to will usually be the same, but they could have a common operator. Authorities and registration authorities can impose extra restrictions on the signing certificate used, for example requiring that the most recently issued signing certificate for a client be used. Some authorities prevent renewal outright, and in that case the response must carry a failure code of noKeyReuse.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a simple form for the common case and a full form for everything else. Renewing a certificate is not a special message; it looks like an ordinary request, signed with the certificate you already have.

sections.title: The Full PKI Request and Its Controls
sections.content:
The Full PKI Request provides the most functionality and flexibility. It is encapsulated in either a signed data or an authenticated data structure, with an encapsulated content type of id-cct-PKIData. A response must always be returned: a simple response if the enrollment succeeded and only certificates are returned, and a full response if information is returned in addition to certificates, if the enrollment is pending, or if it failed.

When signed data is used, the signature can be generated either with the private key material of an embedded signature certification request or with a previously certified signature key. If the private key of a signature certification request is used, the request must include a Subject Key Identifier extension, the subjectKeyIdentifier form of the signer identifier must be used, its value must be the same Subject Key Identifier as in the request, and there must be only one signer in the signed data.

When authenticated data is used, the password recipient info option must be used, a randomly generated key computes the message authentication code over the encapsulated content, and the input to the key derivation algorithm is the concatenation of the identifier, encoded as UTF-8, and the shared secret.

The PKIData content type holds four sequences: a control sequence of tagged attributes, a request sequence of tagged requests, a content sequence of tagged content information, and a sequence of other messages. The controls are the optional pieces that carry the extra services, and there are many of them: status information, identification and identity proof, linking identity and proof-of-possession information, returning data to the client, letting a registration authority modify the request, a transaction identifier and nonces, the encrypted and decrypted proof-of-possession controls, a registration authority proof-of-possession witness, getting a certificate or a revocation list, requesting revocation, registration and response information, querying a pending request, confirming acceptance of a certificate, publishing trust anchors, authenticated data, batch requests and responses, publication information, a control-processed marker, a registration authority identity proof witness, and a response body control.

The status controls carry the outcome. The extended control is the preferred one and the older one is kept for backward compatibility; servers must use the extended control and may additionally use the older one, and clients must be able to process both. The status value is a number: zero for success, two for failed, three for pending, four for noSupport, five for confirmRequired, six for popRequired and seven for partial. The pending and partial values tell the client to poll back, and the control carries a token used in the query pending control and a suggested time at which the server would like to be asked.
sections.plainLanguage: The request is a container with three parts: the controls, the certification requests, and any other content. Each control is a small object with a number that says what it is, and the reply says which part of the request each status applies to.

sections.title: Identity Proof with a Shared Secret
sections.content:
The identification and identity proof controls are how a client proves who it is. The Identity Proof Version 2 control carries the identifier of the hash algorithm used to turn the shared secret into a key, the identifier of the message authentication code algorithm, and the witness value itself.

The method starts with an out-of-band transfer of a token, the shared secret, which should be generated in a random manner; how the token is distributed is beyond the scope of the document. The client then proves its identity in four steps. The PKIData request sequence, encoded exactly as it appears in the request including the sequence type and length, is the value to be validated. A hash of the shared secret as a UTF-8 string is computed using the chosen hash algorithm. A message authentication code is computed, using the value produced in the first step as the message and the value from the second step as the key. The result becomes the witness value in the control.

When the server verifies the control, it computes the same value and compares it with the witness in the request. A registration authority may perform the identity check and tell any following servers that it was successfully performed, using the registration authority identity proof witness control.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and the server share a secret that was handed over separately. The client proves it knows the secret by computing a code over the exact bytes of the request, and the server checks the same code. Because the code covers the request itself, the proof cannot be copied from another request.

sections.title: Proof of Possession for Encryption-Only Keys
sections.content:
Many servers require proof that the entity that generated the certification request actually possesses the private component of the key pair. For keys that can be used as signature keys, signing the certification request with the private key serves as the proof. With keys that can only be used for encryption operations, the proof must be performed by forcing the client to decrypt a value.

By necessity, the proof for an encryption-only key cannot be done in one round trip, since there are four distinct steps. The client tells the server about the public component of a new encryption key pair. The server sends the client a proof-of-possession challenge, encrypted with the presented public encryption key. The client decrypts the challenge using the private key that corresponds to the presented public key and uses it to compute a keyed hash value sent back to the server. The server validates the decrypted challenge and continues processing the certification request.

Two controls carry this. The Encrypted POP control sends the encrypted challenge from the server to the client as part of the response, and holds the request it belongs to, a content info structure, the identifier of the message authentication code algorithm, the identifier of the digest algorithm and the witness. The Decrypted POP control holds the body part identifier, the algorithm identifier and the value the client computed.
sections.plainLanguage: A key that can only encrypt cannot sign anything, so the server has to test it a different way: the server encrypts a challenge with the public key, and only the holder of the private key can read it. That takes two exchanges instead of one.

sections.title: What Changed Since the Earlier Version
sections.content:
The document merges the text of the earlier update document and includes updates inspired by a long list of errata reports against both earlier documents.

To support adopting SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA256, the HMAC-SHA256 algorithm was added to the proof-of-possession algorithms and SHA-256 was added to the witness algorithms, and both were included in the example in the appendix. The section on the encrypted and decrypted proof-of-possession controls was updated to use HMAC-SHA256. The ASN.1 module was updated to import from the 2008 ASN.1 module and was modified to import the password-based key derivation function pseudorandom functions from a new appendix module.

A direct proof-of-possession example was added to address the management of key encapsulation mechanism certificates, and the subject key identifier was added to the examples, with the clarification that the subjectKeyIdentifier choice must be used with the no-signature algorithm. The control attribute table was updated to include the registration authority identity witness and the response body control from the update document. Support was added for the authenticated data structure.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the work was tidying up: merging an earlier update into one document, correcting errata, and adding the newer hash algorithms so that certificates could be issued with them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mechanisms for thwarting replay attacks may be required in particular implementations, depending on the operational environment. Where the authority maintains significant state information, replay attacks may be detectable without the optional nonce mechanisms. Implementers need to consider their environment carefully before choosing whether to implement the sender and recipient nonce controls, and developers of state-constrained clients are strongly encouraged to incorporate them.

Extreme care needs to be taken when archiving a signing key, because the holder of an archived key may be able to use it to generate forged signatures. There are reasons why a signing key should be archived, such as recovering it after a disaster stops the production of revocation lists. Due care must be taken before archiving, since the archiving entity could use the key in a way not conducive to it, and users should be made especially aware that proper verification is made of the certificate used to encrypt the private key material.

Clients and servers need to check cryptographic parameters before issuing certificates to make sure that weak parameters are not used. Implementations ought to be aware of the small subgroup attack when doing parameter validation.

When using a shared secret for authentication, it should be generated using good random number techniques, because user selection of the secret allows dictionary attacks to be mounted. Extreme care must be used when processing the control that publishes trust anchors, because incorrect processing can lead to an attacker changing the set of trusted anchors in order to weaken security. One way of controlling this is for the client to associate each accepted trust anchor with its source and with the types of message for which it is valid, and to accept a new set only if the signature validates, the signer has the required policy approval, and local policy allows it.

The authenticated data structure provides message integrity but does not provide message authentication in all cases. When using message authentication codes, all messages should be for a single entity, because two entities in one message can generate new messages that have a valid code and might be assumed to come from the original sender, and every entity with the shared secret can generate a message that validates, so the secret must be kept secret. Whenever possible the signed data structure should be used in preference.

Any upstream request processor must verify that a registration authority is fully identified and authorised to make the assertion or modification it claims, and reject the request if it is not. Servers need to perform due diligence in checking the contents of a certification request, with special care for names, name forms, algorithm choices and algorithm parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The risks come from the parts the protocol borrows: shared secrets that people choose, signing keys kept in archives, and trust anchors that an attacker would like to replace. The RFC is blunt that the trust anchor control needs the most care.

viz.caption: The status values a reply can carry

items.label: success
items.desc: The request was granted or the action completed.

items.label: failed
items.desc: The request was not granted. More information is included elsewhere in the response.

items.label: pending
items.desc: The request has yet to be processed and the requester must poll back.

items.label: noSupport
items.desc: The requested operation is not supported.

items.label: confirmRequired
items.desc: A confirmation control must be returned before the certificate can be used.

items.label: popRequired
items.desc: A direct proof of possession operation is required.

items.label: partial
items.desc: A partial response is returned and the requester must poll back for the rest.

viz.caption: Proving possession of an encryption-only key, illustrative, not from the RFC

messages.label: Public key
messages.note: Step 1: the client tells the server about the public part of a new encryption key.

messages.label: POP challenge
messages.note: Step 2: the server encrypts a challenge with the presented public key.

messages.label: Keyed hash
messages.note: Step 3: the client decrypts the challenge and returns a keyed hash of it.

messages.label: Certificate
messages.note: Step 4: the server validates the challenge and continues processing the request.

viz.caption: How the shared-secret identity proof is computed

items.title: Start out of band
items.text: A shared secret is handed to the client outside the protocol. How it is distributed is out of scope.

items.title: Hash the secret
items.text: The shared secret is hashed with the chosen hash algorithm to produce a key.

items.title: Code the request
items.text: A message authentication code is computed over the encoded request sequence, using the hashed secret as the key.

items.title: Compare
items.text: The server computes the same value and compares it with the witness carried in the request.

viz.caption: Where the risk sits in a CMC deployment

items.title: Replay attacks
items.text: Mechanisms against replay may be needed depending on the environment, and where the server keeps little state the sender and recipient nonce controls are worth using.

items.title: Archived signing keys
items.text: Extreme care is needed when archiving a signing key, because whoever holds it can forge signatures.

items.title: Weak parameters
items.text: Both ends should check cryptographic parameters before issuing certificates so that weak ones are not used.

items.title: Shared secrets
items.text: A shared secret used for authentication should be generated randomly, because a secret chosen by a person invites dictionary attacks.

items.title: Trust anchors
items.text: The control that publishes trust anchors must be handled carefully, or an attacker can weaken the set of trusted anchors.

items.title: Prefer signatures
items.text: The signed structure should be used in preference to the one based on a message authentication code, and messages should be for a single entity.

items.title: Merged the update document
items.text: The text of the earlier update document is merged in.

items.title: SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA256
items.text: Added to the list of proof-of-possession algorithms and to the witness algorithms.

items.title: Direct proof of possession example
items.text: Added, to address the management of key encapsulation mechanism certificates.

items.title: Authenticated data support
items.text: The protocol now supports the authenticated data structure as well as the signed one.

items.title: New ASN.1 imports
items.text: The module now imports from the 2008 ASN.1 module and from a new appendix module for the password-based key derivation functions.
